headline: High-risk filesystem and browser-enabled coding agent can feed a social-media uploader, creating default-path prompt injection, data leakage, and cascading action errors.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Roo Code reads and writes workspace files and can run browsers, while social-auto-upload consumes local media/account files and uploads via CLI/API. A malicious or malformed artifact from Roo Code could be treated as content by the uploader. The bridge is filesystem-based, so interaction exists without needing exotic setup.
conditions: IF Roo Code writes attacker-controlled text into workspace files that social-auto-upload later parses as upload metadata or captions
IF both agents share the same workspace directory or account file path
mitigations: Use separate directories for code and upload assets
Add a manual review step before any upload job
Restrict Roo Code from writing into the uploader's input folder
requires-engineering: add provenance tags to files before ingestion

B_data_leakage.rationale: Roo Code touches source code and browser screenshots and has broad network egress; social-auto-upload handles video, images, and account data. If they share a workspace, sensitive code or screenshots can be copied into upload inputs or sent out through the uploader's network path. The profiles show a plausible shared-filesystem leak path, so this is not blocked by default.
conditions: IF both agents can access the same workspace or account file directory
IF Roo Code places screenshots or source files into paths that social-auto-upload uploads
mitigations: Keep source-code and upload workspaces separate
Disable automatic inclusion of new files in upload jobs
Review upload manifests before execution
Rotate any exposed account credentials immediately
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent filesystem ACLs

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Roo Code can write the filesystem and modify git state; social-auto-upload cannot write files, so direct write-write conflict is limited. However, Roo Code's workspace-scoped shared state via filesystem can still collide with the uploader's account-file workflow if both operate in the same directory. Uncertainty about the exact shared path pushes this to medium rather than low.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same workspace or account-file directory
IF Roo Code modifies files while social-auto-upload reads them for upload
mitigations: Assign distinct working directories
Pause one agent while the other mutates shared files
Use git branches or copies instead of a shared tree
requires-engineering: add file locking around shared artifacts

D_cascading_error.rationale: Roo Code can generate code, browser-derived content, or file edits that social-auto-upload may treat as ready-to-upload assets. Because the uploader has broad network egress and is designed to act on local files, a bad Roo Code output can cascade into public posting or account-side actions without a strong verification barrier. That makes the default interaction dangerous.
conditions: IF social-auto-upload consumes files produced by Roo Code without human verification
IF Roo Code writes captions, thumbnails, or media that the uploader posts automatically
mitigations: Require human approval before each upload
Validate file names and metadata against a whitelist
Separate draft generation from posting execution
Log and review every outbound upload request
requires-engineering: add schema validation for uploader inputs

E_compliance.rationale: Roo Code handles source code and browser screenshots, while social-auto-upload handles video, images, and account data. The profiles do not specify residency or retention controls, so a compliance mismatch is plausible but not proven. Because both are open-source and the interaction is undocumented, uncertainty remains; medium is appropriate rather than low.
conditions: IF browser screenshots or source code contain regulated personal data
IF account data or media are retained or logged by both tools under different policies
mitigations: Inventory what personal data each agent touches
Set a short retention window for logs and artifacts
Avoid placing regulated data in shared workspaces
Review vendor privacy and retention settings
requires-engineering: document residency and deletion workflows
